{{Short description|Summary of research}}
{{Research}}

'''Secondary research''' involves the summary, collation and/or synthesis of existing research. Secondary research is contrasted with primary research in that primary research involves the generation of data, whereas secondary research uses primary research sources as a source of data for analysis.<ref name=ithaca>{{cite web|title=Primary and Secondary Sources|url=https://libguides.ithaca.edu/research101/primary|website=library.ithaca.edu}}</ref>  A notable marker of primary research is the inclusion of a "methods" section, where the authors describe how the data was generated.

Common examples of secondary research include [[textbooks]], [[encyclopedia]]s, [[news]] articles, [[review articles]], and [[meta analysis|meta analyses]].<ref>{{cite web|last1=Ormsby|first1=Tim|title=Search Smart: Types of Research: Secondary Research|url=http://flinders.libguides.com/researchtypes/secondary|website=flinders.libguides.com|language=en|access-date=2018-03-13|archive-date=2020-12-01|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201201061217/https://flinders.libguides.com/researchtypes/secondary|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last1=Andrews|first1=Camille|title=LibGuides: Scholarly Literature Types: Primary vs. Secondary Articles|url=https://guides.library.cornell.edu/c.php?g=293669&p=2004549|website=guides.library.cornell.edu|language=en}}</ref>

When conducting secondary research, authors may draw data from published academic papers, government documents, [[Statistical database|statistical databases]], and historical records.<ref name=ithaca/><ref>{{cite web|last1=Bosch|first1=Eileen|title=LibGuides: Library Basics: Primary and Secondary Sources|url=http://libguides.bgsu.edu/c.php?g=227153&p=1505675|website=libguides.bgsu.edu|language=en}}</ref>

== Fields ==
The term is widely used in fields such as history, [[legal research]], [[market research]], and Wikipedia editing. The principal methodology in health secondary research is the [[systematic review]], commonly using meta-analytic statistical techniques. Other methods of synthesis, like realist reviews and meta-[[narrative]] reviews, have been developed in the 21st century.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Greenhalgh |first1=Trisha |last2=Robert |first2=Glenn |last3=Macfarlane |first3=Fraser |last4=Bate |first4=Paul |last5=Kyriakidou |first5=Olivia |date=2004 |title=Diffusion of innovations in service organizations: systematic review and recommendations |journal=[[Milbank Quarterly]] |volume=82 |issue=4 |pages=581–629 |pmid=15595944 |pmc=2690184 |doi=10.1111/j.0887-378X.2004.00325.x}}</ref>

Secondary market research includes the reuse by a second party of any data collected from a first party such as telephone interviews or surveys. Secondary market research can be broken up into two categories: information from internal sources such as an agency or company, and information from external sources held outside an organization or agency.<ref>DeVault, G. (2019, June 25). Differences Between Primary and Secondary Market Research. Retrieved from https://www.thebalancesmb.com/what-is-secondary-market-research-2296890</ref> Secondary market research uses information from the past, reuses data already collected, and is more economical.

== Primary research vs secondary research ==

[[Research#Forms of research|Primary research]] is research that is collected firsthand and is original to the person using it.<ref name="Driscoll">{{cite book |last=Driscoll |first=Dana Lynn |date=2010 |chapter=Introduction to primary research: observations, surveys, and interviews |editor1-last=Lowe |editor1-first=Charles |editor2-last=Zemliansky |editor2-first=Pavel |title=Writing Spaces: Readings on Writing |volume=2 |location=West Lafayette, Ind. |publisher=Parlor Press |pages=153–174 |chapter-url=https://wac.colostate.edu/docs/books/writingspaces2/driscoll--introduction-to-primary-research.pdf |url=https://wac.colostate.edu/books/writingspaces/writingspaces2/ |isbn=9781602351844 |oclc=677865118}}</ref> When conducting primary research, the goal is to answer questions that have not been answered in the published literature.<ref name="Driscoll"/> Additionally, the research has to be verified by others to help eliminate one's own biases.<ref name="ReferenceA">{{cite journal |last=Church |first=Russell M. |date=February 2002 |title=The effective use of secondary data |journal=Learning and Motivation |volume=33 |issue=1 |pages=32–45 |doi=10.1006/lmot.2001.1098}}</ref> Primary research can be a survey, observation, or an interview. This type of research tends to be more time consuming and can be costly.<ref name="McCrocklin">McCrocklin, S. (2018, October 4). Primary vs. Secondary Research. Retrieved from https://www.geopoll.com/blog/primary-vs-secondary-research/</ref> If possible, secondary research should be done before primary research.

Secondary research is based on already published data and information gathered from other conducted studies.<ref name="ReferenceA"/> It is a common practice by researchers to conduct secondary research before primary research in order to determine what information is not already available.<ref name="McCrocklin"/> Secondary research is an easy place to start when starting a new research project. Secondary research can vary in credibility depending on where the data is coming from and who is sharing research.<ref>Treadwell, D. F. (2016). Introducing communication research: paths of inquiry. Thousand Oaks, CA: SAGE Publications.</ref>
